title: It Rains Brilliants
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later boards reviewed. Begin after ...axb6, immediately before g8=Q at 175 seconds, with the complete eight-piece later diagram: White Kd8/a6/b7/c6/g7 against Kb8/b6/c7. The source promotion and b5 reply are visible; subsequent king routes and captures are explicitly independent representative completions. A finite legal strategy covers every Black defense after g8=Q and ends in exact seven-piece wins. Earlier queen sacrifice, knight route, rook blockade, king march and pawn diversion remain outside this proof. The b6 pawn is the black a7 pawn after axb6, not a missing spare pawn.
transcript: Black's brilliant idea is rook to h8. Now, attacking the knight [music] and threatening a checkmate in just one move. If white tries to save the position by taking this pawn, preventing the checkmate, now after the rook takes the knight and the king goes up, black has the brilliant shot rook to a1, sacrificing the rook completely. But of course, once the rook is taken by the king, this is going to be a stalemate. So it seems like black has successfully saved this position and it is going to be able to hold the draw. And [music] it would be like that if it wasn't for an incredible resource that white has in this position. The absolutely incredible and mind-blowing queen to f8, sacrificing the queen completely. And [music] yet, after the rook takes, we start to see the plan of white unfolding. It might seem like black is creating the same exact threat of checkmate. And if we move the knight, it's going to sacrifice the rook for the stalemate. But we have to realize that this black rook can never actually leave the last rank without giving [music] a check because if it does, well, we're going to promote here with a checkmate. [music] So the brilliant plan of white is to bring the knight by sacrificing it with a knight to f2. And of course, the knight cannot be taken. But the rook can of course try to create again the checkmate threat. We can still block it with knight to h3, sacrificing the knight again. So black has to become creative with rook to g8. And now after the knight moves to f4, it can pin it with rook to f8. And now of course, if the knight moves, this is actually going to be a checkmate and black would win. But luckily, white can place black in zugzwang with a brilliant king to b1, sacrificing the knight yet again and maintaining it blocking the view of the rook. So it has to go back to creating the checkmate threat. But again, the knight can simply sacrifice itself. But now, after the rook moves, the knight doesn't have a safe square to go to anymore. But white is the chosen one for a reason. And so he plays knight to f6 anyway. Black has to to the sacrifice because if he doesn't, now we have gotten the knight in the perfect position to promote this pawn to a queen finally. And after the rook takes, we can give this check, and the only move for black is to take the knight, allowing us to bring this other pawn to the promotion square and win like this. It's important [music] to remember that the black rook can never leave the last rank, and white has all of the time to start moving this pawn. So, the next phase of the plan is to start bringing the king, [music] and black can only move the black pawn, but eventually the white king is going to be able to pick it up. And now black is yet again forced [music] to move this rook. None of the other pieces can move, meaning that it has to shuffle back and forth between these two squares, while the king goes to the next plan of picking up this pawn. It continues to march down this path, now advancing the pawn, finally bringing the king all the way to the perfect position to now sacrifice a pawn to give black the option to make more moves. Now, after the rook moves, we're going to come to attack it, and now we can finally get it off the board. White can get another queen and very easily win this game.
